Q: check for user id in model that adds data to the wait table or model that grabs data for the home page or use two queries? A:

Your database design is wrong. You should create a separate user table with user-specific data (name, image, ...) plus a user_id and a wait table with general information (name, desc, map, ...) that doesn't use user-specific information except user_id.

If your database isn't too large you can use a select tag with valid user_ids so you don't need validation.

To know the user_ids not in wait, use a similar query:

SELECT user.userid
FROM user
LEFT JOIN wait ON user.userid = wait.userid
WHERE ISNULL(wait.place_id)

These userids can be put into a select-list.

Q: Launch a terminal command in Go that is defined as an alias A:

if have your alias/funcions in file that is not the .bashrc, you can reference that as described below via "{ source ~/.bashrc;"+shellcommand+";}", and do not need to touch your .bashrc at all. for me, since the .bashrc is sufficiently complex it was easier to include the if ... then ...fi around the top than doing that directly.

if you want to actually make referencing the .bashrc work, this is what works, with the additional bonus that you can pass your shell call directly without resorting to "--foo", "bar", "--like", "this" as all the other libs or examples force you to but lets you pass it like "--foo bar --like this" directly:

the actual trick is to NOT DO any of these in your golang code as none of them seem to work properly or get the ~/.bashrc to be read at all:

  • starting an interactive bash session by using the -i as this will cause infighting over the terminal depending on what is going on in there

  • starting a -l login shell

  • appending the existing environment with the BASH_ENV var:

    cmd.Env=append(os.Environ(),"BASH_ENV="+os.Getenv("HOME")+"/.bashrc")

  • using an --rcfile flag i.e. cmd:=exec.Command("/bin/bash","--rcfile","~/.bashrc","-i","-c",command)

likely you have something like this in your ~/.bashrc written near the top preventing commands further down from being sourced due to the return:

# If not running interactively, don't do anything
case $- in
    *i*) ;;
      *) return;;
esac

the actual solution to get the .bashrc sourced has two dimensions:

1. getting the bashrc to actually be read at all from inside the go src and passing an environment var as flag the session that is started when the bash interpreter is being called:

  • sourcing the .bashrc inside the shell command that is passed to the interpreter via -c

  • . / source and your actual command have to be grouped together via i.e. a list (...) or a grouped command { ...;} : (mind the space, replace the dots)

    "{ source ~/.bashrc;"+shellcommand+";}",

  • inject an env var via the os/exec.Command()-build environment, as this cannot be done via bash parameters directly and since --rcfile doesnt work either there are not many other options:

    const SCRIPTENVFLAG=`SCRIPTENV="1"`

    cmd.Env=append(os.Environ(),SCRIPTENVFLAG)

2. fixing the actual bash environment:

  • fixing your bashrc to skip the -i check-induced return that prevents anything else from being loaded, easiest done by wrapping it into an if block, toggling on the env var injected above:

    if [[ $SCRIPTENV == "1" ]]
then
    case $- in
        *i*) ;;
        *) return;;
    esac



   ... a lot of stuff to skip ...


fi

# here now should be your includes and aliases

  • close the if block shortly before your other . or alias command definitions, as you probably have added your relevant parts to the end of the ~/.bashrc

  • this is to make sure you do not define anything that is relevant to an interactive shell but will break non-interactive ones, effectively duplicating the -i check but not working the $- contents so it will not skip the complete file

runnable golang example, if you get the libraries: (go mod init main, go mod tidy in your projectfolder with the source file, or remove the libraries if you dont want them)

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "github.com/gookit/color"
    l "github.com/sirupsen/logrus"
    "time"

    "bytes"
    "os"
    "os/exec"
    //"strings"
    //"github.com/google/shlex"
    //sq "github.com/Hellseher/go-shellquote"
)

const SCRIPTENVFLAG=`SCRIPTENV="1"`
const SHELLEXECUTABLE=`/bin/bash`
//const SHELLFLAGS=`-xc`
const SHELLFLAGS=`-c`

func bash(shellcommand string) (string){
    cmd:=exec.Command(
        SHELLEXECUTABLE,
        SHELLFLAGS,
        "{ source ~/.bashrc;"+shellcommand+";}",
    )
    cmd.Env=append(os.Environ(),SCRIPTENVFLAG)
    //cmd.Env=append(os.Environ(),"BASH_ENV="+os.Getenv("HOME")+"/.bashrc")
    var stdout,stderr bytes.Buffer
    cmd.Stdout=&stdout
    cmd.Stderr=&stderr
    err:=cmd.Run()
    stderrcolor:=color.New(color.OpBold,color.FgLightRed,color.BgBlack)
    if stderr.String()!=""{stderrcolor.Println(stderr.String())}
    errcolor:=color.New(color.OpBold,color.FgYellow,color.BgBlack)
    if err!=nil{errcolor.Println(err)}
    return stdout.String()
}

func main() {
    pp:=color.New(color.OpBold,color.FgLightWhite,color.BgLightRed)
    pp.Println(`testcode ...`)
    starttime:=time.Now()
    l.SetReportCaller(true)
    l.SetLevel(l.WarnLevel)
    l.SetLevel(l.InfoLevel)

    fmt.Println(bash(`ls`))
    fmt.Println(bash(`ll`))
    fmt.Println(bash(`ls -alh --color=none`))
    fmt.Println(bash("pwd"))
    fmt.Println(bash(">&2 echo stderr test"))
    fmt.Println(bash("grep SCRIPTENV ~/.bashrc"))
    fmt.Println(bash(`printf "$SCRIPTENV is set to %s" $SCRIPTENV`))
    fmt.Println(bash("ping -c1 1.1"))

    endtime:=time.Now()
    fmt.Println("\nruntime",endtime.Sub(starttime))
}

Q: Perl autoincrement of string not working as before A:

As others have pointed out, the string is being using in numeric context at some point. This causes ++ to treat it as a number, converting "ZCLK0" to 0, then incrementing that. ( BTW, "ZCKL1" would also be converted to 0).

So to preserve as many features of string ++ that I can think of, use the following code:

$str = 1 unless $str =~ s{^([[:alpha:]]*[[:digit:]]+)\z}
                         { my $tmp = $1; ++$tmp }e;

This looks uses s///e to make sure the string contains letters followed by numbers. It then creates a temporary variable and increments that. If the s///e fails, it sets $str to 1.

s{}{}e is used as a reminder that the right-hand side is an eval{}.

Q: How can I debug (step into) BinaryFormatter.Deserialize()? A:

tl;dr: A different version of a compiler (or different settings?) may generate different names for the generated method corresponding to an anonymous function. If such a method is pointed by a private field of a serialized class, you get the exception, even though the source didn't change between the two builds.

I just tracked the exact type of situation, but with the deserialization triggered in an ASP.NET application's session. Like this case, the BinaryFormatter is used.

<.ctor>b__0 corresponds to the generated method corresponding to an anonymous function.

Now, the problem here is the dependency on such a method during serialization, because the name is not guaranteed to be the same over different builds (even with an unchanged source). This almost surely tracks to some kind of delegate in a private instance field of a serialized class. Note that such the class where the anonymous function is declared is not necessarily the class that holds the reference to that function in a private field.

Unfortunately, I didn't have time to track why the same source produces different names for the anonymous function, but given the history of the project involved it is either a different compiler version of the options passed to it. I am convinced it is the earlier.

If you have access to the assemblies in both sides, you can confirm the change. At first, I tried exporting the dissembled source of both assemblies in dotPeek and then doing a diff of the folders. That didn't prove a good process, but it may be due to some dotPeek settings that need to be set or something.

Using a combination of NDepend and Reflector worked better. You can do an assembly comparison of the earlier. I changed one of the builds in queries to get all constructors of serialized classes that had any kind of change. This narrowed it down to a few classes/constructors (there is a risk of not catching it this way, if the anonymous function was created in a non-serializable class).

Once I had it down to a few constructors, from NDepend I opened an old vs. new comparison that uses Reflector for it. This not only showed the method name in the same format as the exception, but it already showed got me to the right one in the code base.

Once I 'new' the class, I found it better to open each assembly in a separate ReSharper window and see the methods of the class. It is quite visible there.

Also note that in the case where the code is changed, even the same compiler version/option may give you different names, so it is very brittle to have private fields in serializable classes that point to functions. The following answer expands on it: Could we save delegates in a file (C#)?
